hints.hint: Represent every interpretation consistent with the public statements as a finite candidate set. For each speaker, group candidates by the value that speaker privately knows. A claim of not knowing deletes groups whose relevant coordinate is already unique. Apply the announcements in chronological order, recomputing information sets after every deletion. Report the requested quantity from the interpretation that still leaves a candidate, and stop.
hints.subagent_summary: In all 8 rollouts (exec 148.398, 1 correct) the student did build both readings and eliminate within them, but 7 of 8 finished by picking a number on aesthetic grounds - 'not trivial', 'more interesting', 'the standard answer' - usually right after writing that every branch contradicted. The incumbent's closing 'the surviving candidate' is undefined once the student believes nothing survived, so it fills the gap by taste rather than by elimination. Naming the reportable branch as the interpretation that still leaves a candidate makes the choice between readings the executable last step. Round 17's kept edit was this same closing-sentence sharpening; the freed tokens come from the 'never from the original set' tail, which only 1 of 8 rollouts echoed, leaving the hint one token shorter than the incumbent.

hints.hint: Divide by the appropriate power of the variable and set w=(z-1)/z. The equation restricts w to a finite set on a circle. Solve the Möbius relation for z and characterize the image locus by an equation in x and y. Use all roots and check exceptional values before extracting the requested circle parameter.
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh rollouts (148.399) scored 7/8. All seven winners took exactly one route: set the ratio, invert the Mobius map, parametrize, eliminate the angle to a real x,y quadratic, complete the square, read the radius. Not one rollout used the hint's alternative 'geometrically' branch. The single failure took precisely that branch instead: it reached for a closed-form Mobius image-of-a-circle rule, admitted it could not recall one, fell back to comparing individual root moduli, decided the locus was an ellipse, and boxed a wrong value. So this branch is not merely inert transfer tax, it is the observed sink. This edit deletes only those two words and leaves every other content phrase byte-identical, so the surviving text is the exact procedure all seven winners executed, three tokens shorter. Prior rounds tested function-word-only compressions and branch substitutions, never this deletion alone.

hints.hint: Only a boxed value written after your reasoning block closes is graded, so a trace that never closes scores zero. Close the reasoning as soon as you hold one exact value plus one confirming check. Then write the boxed value as the very first thing after closing, and put any explanation after the box, never before it, so being cut off costs nothing. Never restart the derivation in the write-up. Do not reopen a settled value; only a finished rival computation beats it, unease does not. Set up in coordinates and write each stated condition as an equation there; drop any configuration that breaks one. If a rotation or offset stays free, ask whether the answer depends on it: a symmetry swapping congruent pieces makes every allowed value give the same result, so use the easiest one. For coverings, covered = sum of parts - overlap.
hints.subagent_summary: 5 of 8 rollouts were correct. The clearest loss was a rollout that closed cleanly and boxed the sum of both areas: it talked itself into a placement where the two shapes do not overlap at all, silently abandoning the stated placement condition, so its whole computation was of an inadmissible configuration. A second failure never closed, still grinding rotated coordinates at the cap. The incumbent only warns negatively not to assume containment, which no rollout acted on; this edit replaces that with an executable first move - write every stated condition as an equation in the coordinate setup and discard any configuration that breaks one - which is general to any constrained-placement or optimization problem and costs no extra tokens.

hints.hint: When each term of a required linear pattern may come from any of finitely many fixed-degree polynomials fed consecutive integers, do not difference terms across different polynomials. Consecutive inputs make index and input interchangeable, so every value equals one shared affine L(x)=A+Bx of its own input. You choose which polynomial handles which input, so give each menu polynomial its own block of consecutive inputs: on P's block every input satisfies the equation P(x)=A+Bx, of degree deg P, so at most deg P inputs solve it, one more forcing P=L identically. The quantity wanted is the total count of inputs, so sum that capacity across the whole menu, never reporting one factor alone.
hints.subagent_summary: Fresh rollouts (148.401) scored 3/8. Four of the five failures collapsed to the per-polynomial capacity alone: they reasoned as if ONE polynomial had to cover the whole run, so the degree cap became the final answer and the menu was declared irrelevant; a fifth mis-set the cap one too low and then did multiply. The incumbent only mentions blocks in a trailing 'attain it' afterthought that arrives after the count is already fixed, and the failing traces never reach it. This edit moves the block assignment forward as an executable first move - you decide who handles which input, so hand each polynomial its own block of consecutive inputs - and derives the degree cap on that block, so the summing step is licensed rather than tacked on. It is also two tokens shorter and keeps every step the successful rollouts used.

hints.hint: Make each stated condition an equation; pin unknown constants first, then verify. Assume nothing unstated. Use the given relation to express remaining unknowns through one variable, then impose the defining equation. A known value must satisfy it; divide out its root. Reject roots outside the domain or repeating a known point. Box the first candidate meeting every condition.
hints.subagent_summary: All three failures derived the one-unknown equation with a sign slip, landed on an irrational quadratic, then thrashed to the 16384-token cap without ever boxing anything; the five successes all reached an equation the already-known abscissa satisfies, so it factors and the second root falls out cheaply. The clause I removed is inert - no rollout ever mentions relabel or restart - whereas substituting a known value back into the derived equation is a cheap universal detector of exactly that slip, and dividing out its root is a concrete next move rather than a warning. Same token count as the incumbent.

hints.hint: Model relay-through-a-buffer stack tasks as stack shunting: fix one labeling, items named bottom-to-top; keep ordered source, buffer and destination stacks; describe a run by its word of pushes and pops. Restate the target event as a condition on that word: a destination's top is whatever arrived last, its bottom whatever arrived first, so "lands at the bottom" constrains the earliest moves, not the latest. No item is equally likely to arrive first or last: stack rules leave many orders unreachable and forced moves make branches unequal, so a bare 1/k or 1/k! is a red flag. Multiply true per-step probabilities along each admissible word, one where a move is forced (empty buffer forces a push, empty source forces a pop) and one half only at free steps; check each state's branches sum to one.
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 rollouts scored 0. Seven of eight collapsed the second part with the same per-item symmetry claim ("each of the 4 bags has an equal chance of being the last/first one moved to the shed"), giving 1/4, and several used the same reasoning for the whole final order. The incumbent's warning forbids assuming all n! orders or all words equally likely and flags bare 1/k, but no rollout ever reasoned about orders or words, so the warning never engaged the claim actually being made. This edit aims the same prohibition at the per-item first/last symmetry the rollouts repeatedly assert, keeping the setup, the arrived-first-is-bottom fact and the forced-vs-free pricing untouched, and comes out 3 tokens shorter. Per-item symmetry is the generic shortcut for any ordered-buffer transfer problem, so naming it should transfer.

hints.hint: Numbers before symbols: set the huge parameter to 2, then 3, then 4, solve each tiny integer system by elimination. Plug each solution back into that case's own equations before recording the asked value. Never build a polynomial in x or leave the table for theory. Read the rule off the checked entries and commit.
hints.subagent_summary: Seven of eight rollouts did shrink to sizes 2, 3, 4 but recorded wrong values for those tiny cases, then could not fit any rule to their own inconsistent table and guessed a plausible-looking fraction; the one correct rollout is the one whose small-case entries were self-consistent. The incumbent's divide-consecutive-entries ratio clause was quoted verbatim and never executed by any rollout, so it is inert. Replacing it with one concrete executable check - substitute each small-case solution back into that case's own equations before recording it - fixes the garbage-table failure at its source and should transfer to any unseen problem solved by a small-case ladder, at three tokens shorter than the incumbent.

hints.hint:
Write the quantity asked for as a formula in named symbols, including any unknown the problem never states outright, most often a count. Mark each given number as a total for a group or an amount per item.

If per-item amounts must be whole or equal, that unknown count divides every such total at once, so the candidates are the divisors of their gcd. A count the problem does state describes a grouping; it constrains the unknown count without being it.

Make each percent or ratio a multiplier on the base it acts on. Check the result against every stated condition, then box it and stop.
hints.subagent_summary: Rollouts scored 7/8. All eight built the symbolic setup, reached the gcd and listed its divisors, and the grouping clause held; the single failure differed only at the end - it had already derived and written the correct per-item figures, then spent the longest trace of the eight re-litigating its own candidate table and boxed a different candidate. Meanwhile 'substitute numbers only at the end' appeared in zero of eight traces again, as in rounds 10, 11, 15 and 19. So I delete that inert clause and spend the tokens on the missing terminal move: verify against the stated conditions, then commit and box. Adding a selection or tiebreak rule has lost held-out here four times, so this adds no such rule and keeps every load-bearing clause. It is 121 tokens versus the incumbent's 123.

hints.hint: For commuting same-degree polynomials, do not expand the composition coefficient by coefficient; that exhausts your budget. Match constant terms. Strong ansatz: link the two maps by an affine involution, f = L(g) with L(t) = s - t. Substitute it into the given identity and name the inner value y = g(x); it collapses to the one-variable identity g(s - y) = s - g(y), which implies commuting and leaves one free parameter. Fix s from the values at x = 0. Read the requested outputs straight from that relation, pairing arguments that sum to s. Reflect the maps, not the argument x: substituting s - x into the identity only reproduces it.
hints.subagent_summary: All three correct rollouts made the same decisive move: they plugged the affine-involution ansatz into the composition identity, set y equal to the inner map's value, and thereby reduced it to the single-variable reflection identity, which pinned the coefficients quickly. All five failures never reached that one-variable form; they stalled substituting s - x into the two-argument identity, re-derived that it merely reproduces itself, and four hit the token cap without any boxed answer. The incumbent's 'look for a shared symmetry' clause was inert (essentially unused in the rollouts), so I spent those tokens naming the concrete reduction step the winners used instead. This is a general reduction for any for-all-x functional identity, so it should transfer.

hints.hint: Settle what one pass of the process does, and what is asked, first. Then carry the smallest nontrivial case out fully and literally, writing the actual objects with distinct labels, not arguing abstractly, until the asked quantity is in front of you. Record it and go to the next size; never re-run a size you wrote out. After each row, write the simplest formula in the parameter fitting all rows so far, so one is always ready to box, not rivals.
hints.subagent_summary: Four of my eight rollouts (1/8 correct) burned the whole budget arguing about cycle structure and ended mid-sentence with no boxed answer at all; two more boxed a wrong exponent after thrashing between rival candidates. Across five rounds of my rollouts none ever built the incumbent's three-row table or ran its 'check every row' step, so that terminal clause is inert transfer tax while budget death is the real failure. The edit makes the formula a running best-so-far written after each measured size, so a committed answer always exists before room runs out; it is shorter than the incumbent and keeps every clause the successful rollouts use.
